newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-ERA says new mines no worry.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-ERA says new mines no worry.

text.p: Energy Resources of Australia Ltd (ERA) chief executive Phillip Shirvington said on Friday he was not concerned about the impact on the uranium miner of possible new Australian competitors.
Shirvington said ERA had estimated any new Australian mines could reduce uranium prices by about eight percent, but this was not enough to eat into the company's profits.
"If new mines come on in Australia, it could to some extent cause prices to soften, but from a very high plateau," Shirvington told Reuters in an interview.
"I believe it was around a possible eight percent fall from a high level as a result of the introduction of new uranium mines in Australia," he said.
"But that is something that we can easily live with. We would still be very profitable."
Australia's conservative government overturned the previous Labor government's three-mines policy shortly after it came into power on March 2.
Under the three-mines policy, Australia was able to supply only about 11 percent of the world uranium market, despite having about 29 percent of total global reserves.
The new government has identified 18 major uranium deposits which could be developed as new mines to take advantage of surging uranium prices.

Uranium was trading at a spot price of around US$15.40 a pound at October 31, compared to about US$11.00 a pound at the beginning of the 1995/96 year and Shirvington said there was substantial room for further increases.

"The fundamentals are suggesting that there will be a shortage of uranium at least until the year 2000 because there simply aren't enough uranium mines in the world operating to supply the demand," he said.
"Until more mines come into production, that'll continue to be the situation which will put (upwards) pressure on prices."
However, he repeated chairman Campbell Anderson's October statement that the uranium miner expected flat earnings in 1996/97 with an improvement in the following year.
ERA, 68 percent owned by North Ltd, reported an operating profit of A$58.56 million for the year to June 30, 1996, up from A$35.42 million in the previous year.
It posted a net profit of A$40.73 million for the 1995/96 year, compared with A$12.37 million previously.

Shirvington said ERA would lift production at its Ranger mine in the Northern Territory to 5,000 tonnes a year from a current 3,500 when it completed expansion of the mine's mill capacity by July next year.
"Given the outlook for strong prices, we believe that that will certainly impact favourably on ERA but we won't see that until the 1997/98 financial year," he said.
ERA is 68 percent owned by North Ltd. At 0300 GMT (1.00 p.m.) the uranium miner's shares were steady at A$6.05 while North shares were one cent lower at A$3.54.
